    return dt.strftime("%I:%M%p").lstrip("0")

 – the minimum meeting duration.
2. List the travel times between all locations.

4. For each friend you plan on meeting, calculate the travel time from your current location. Then determine the optimal departure time from the current location such that you arrive as close as possible to the start of the friend’s availability window (avoiding long idle waiting times if possible).
5. Once you arrive early you wait until the friend’s available start time, then meet them for at least the minimum required duration.
6. After the meeting, check that you still have time to travel to the next friend’s location and meet them within their window.
7. Evaluate possible orders and choose the schedule that allows you to meet the most friends (or the one that minimizes wasted waiting time while satisfying all constraints).

from datetime import datetime, timedelta

# Helper function to format time as H:MMAM/PM without a leading zero.

    ('Sunset District', 'Pacific Heights'): 21,
    ('Sunset District', 'Financial District'): 30,
    ('Pacific Heights', 'Sunset District'): 21,
    ('Pacific Heights', 'Financial District'): 13,
    ('Financial District', 'Sunset District'): 31,
    ('Financial District', 'Pacific Heights'): 13
}

# Define the meeting events with time windows and required durations.

    "Kevin": {
        "location": "Financial District",
        "available_start": datetime.strptime("11:30AM", "%I:%M%p"),
        "available_end": datetime.strptime("1:45PM", "%I:%M%p"),
        "min_meeting": 75  # in minutes
    },
    "Rebecca": {
        "location": "Pacific Heights",
        "available_start": datetime.strptime("2:15PM", "%I:%M%p"),
        "available_end": datetime.strptime("9:30PM", "%I:%M%p"),
        "min_meeting": 15  # in minutes
    }
}

# 2. Then, after meeting Kevin, go to Pacific Heights for Rebecca.

    # There is waiting time at the start location.
    schedule_steps.append(f"You wait until {format_time(departure_time_for_kevin)} at {start_location}.")

schedule_steps.append(f"You meet Kevin for {events['Kevin']['min_meeting']} minutes from {format_time(meeting_start_kevin)} to {format_time(meeting_end_kevin)} in Financial District.")

  – whether you arrive during his/her availability window,
  – and whether the meeting (arrival time plus required meeting duration) finishes before the friend’s availability ends.
 • Also account for idle/waiting time if you arrive early.

 • List each friend’s location, available time window, and required meeting duration.
 • List travel times between all locations.

 • At each leg compute:
  – The departure time (which may be determined by the end of the previous meeting).
  – The travel duration to the next friend’s location.
  – An arrival time.
  – A possible waiting period if you arrive too early for that friend’s window.
  – Then schedule a meeting lasting at least the minimum required, checking that the meeting end time is within the window.

You must “route‐schedule” your day so that each chosen friend’s meeting can be started (after travel and any waiting) and then run for at least the required number of minutes while staying inside that friend’s available time window. In our case your day begins at 9:00AM at Embarcadero and you have four friends with these availabilities (times are measured in minutes after midnight):

 • Jeffrey is at Chinatown from 7:00AM (420) to 7:45AM (465) – must meet him for at least 30 minutes.

 • Joseph is at Golden Gate Park from 5:30PM (1050) to 9:15PM (1275) – at least 120 minutes.
 • Deborah is at Union Square from 6:00PM (1080) to 7:45PM (1185) – at least 90 minutes.

A quick look shows that although Jeffrey’s visit is “on‐the morning” (before 9:00AM), you cannot catch him if you start at 9:00AM. Also note that Joseph’s and Deborah’s windows are in the early evening but (with travel time) there is no way to “chain” the 120‐minute meeting with Joseph and then get to Deborah in time for a full 90‐minute meeting (or vice–versa). Hence the best you can do is to plan a schedule that meets two friends. (You could choose Lisa plus one of the evening friends.) 

One “optimal” solution is for you to plan your afternoon so that you meet Lisa exactly at the start of her window and then later catch one of the evening friends. In the code below we use a “search‐over‐schedules” (depth–first search) approach. In each “move” we note that if you are at a current location and time and want to go meet a friend at a certain location, you are allowed to wait (either at your current location–delaying departure so that you time your travel just right – or wait on arrival) so that you start the friend’s meeting exactly no earlier than his/her available start. (We “choose” to use the minimum meeting duration exactly.) Then, if the meeting finishes before the friend’s available end time you update your “state” (new current time is the end of that meeting and your location is the friend’s location) and try to add another meeting.

    hours = minutes // 60
    mins = minutes % 60
    period = "AM"

        period = "PM"
    display_hour = hours
    if hours == 0:
        display_hour = 12
    elif hours > 12:
        display_hour = hours - 12

        "available_end": time_in_minutes("6:45PM"),      # 6:45PM

    "Steven": {

        "available_start": time_in_minutes("4:30PM"),  # 4:30PM
        "available_end": time_in_minutes("6:45PM"),      # 6:45PM
        "duration": 60
    }
}

current_time = time_in_minutes("9:00AM")  # 540 minutes

schedule.append(f"You start at {current_location} at {minutes_to_time(current_time)}.")

# We choose the order: Karen -> Elizabeth -> Anthony -> Steven
order = ["Karen", "Elizabeth", "Anthony", "Steven"]

for friend in order:
    details = friends[friend]
    friend_location = details["location"]
    # Travel to friend's location from current_location
    travel_time = travel_times[current_location][friend_location]
    depart_time = current_time
    arrival_time = depart_time + travel_time
    schedule.append(f"You travel to {friend_location} in {travel_time} minutes and arrive at {minutes_to_time(arrival_time)}.")
    
    # Wait until friend is available (if necessary)
    meeting_start = max(arrival_time, details["available_start"])
    if meeting_start > arrival_time:
        schedule.append(f"You wait until {minutes_to_time(meeting_start)}.")
    
    meeting_end = meeting_start + details["duration"]
    # Check that meeting finishes before the friend's availability window ends.
    if meeting_end > details["available_end"]:
        schedule.append(f"Unfortunately, you cannot meet {friend} for the required {details['duration']} minutes within their available window.")
        break
    schedule.append(f"You meet {friend} for {details['duration']} minutes from {minutes_to_time(meeting_start)} to {minutes_to_time(meeting_end)}.")
    
    # Update current location and time
    current_location = friend_location
    current_time = meeting_end

# Print the schedule list.
print(schedule)

  c. The meeting must start no later than the friend’s available start time such that the meeting (including its minimum duration) is fully contained in the friend’s availability window.

            max_meetings = num_meetings

Below is our “thought‐process” and general approach followed by a complete Python script.

──────────────────────────────
General Reasoning & Method:

1. Define the problem “state” as being at a given location at a given time. (We start at 9:00AM in the Financial District, i.e. time = 540 minutes after midnight.)

2. For each friend there is a location, an available time‐window (start and end times in minutes from midnight) and a minimum meeting duration. Also, travel times (in minutes) between every pair of locations are provided (note that the travel times are not fully symmetric).

3. To “build a schedule” we need to decide on an ordering (route) of visits. For each friend:
   • From our current state, add the travel time from the current location to the friend’s location.
   • The friend is “available” only after a given time. Thus, if you arrive early you must wait until the friend’s start time.
   • The meeting begins at the later of (arrival time, friend’s start time) and lasts the required minimum meeting duration. The meeting must finish before or exactly at the friend’s cutoff time.
   
4. We use a Depth‐First Search (DFS) (or backtracking) approach. Starting at Financial District at 9:00AM, we try every possible friend visit in any order that meets the timing constraints.
   • For each remaining friend we compute:
       – arrival_time = current_time + travel_time from the current location.
       – meeting_start = max(arrival_time, friend_available_start)
       – meeting_finish = meeting_start + meeting_duration.
       – Feasibility: meeting_finish must be ≤ friend_available_end.
   • If feasible, we add messages detailing:
       – The travel step (e.g., “You travel from X to Y in Z minutes and arrive at HH:MMAM/PM.”)
       – A “wait” step if arrival is before the available start.
       – A “meeting” step (e.g., “You meet [Name] for [duration] minutes from HH:MM to HH:MM.”)
   • We then update our state (with the new current location and time) and continue the DFS with the remaining friends.
   
5. Our optimization goal is to “meet as many friends as possible.” Thus the DFS is aimed at finding a schedule that visits the maximum number of friends from our list. (In our example we eventually can visit all 5 in the order: Kimberly → Timothy → Andrew → Patricia → Deborah.)

6. Finally, we print a schedule – a list of strings following a format similar to:
   ["You start at Financial District at 9:00AM.", 
    "You travel from Financial District to Chinatown in 5 minutes and arrive at 9:05AM.",
    "You wait until 10:15AM.",

        # Compute travel from current location to this friend's location.
        travel = travel_times[current_location][friend_loc]
        arrival = current_time + travel
        # The meeting cannot start before the friend’s available start.

        meeting_finish = meeting_start + friend["duration"]
        # Check if the meeting can be finished within the friend’s availability window.

            new_schedule = deepcopy(schedule)

            travel_msg = f"You travel from {current_location} to {friend_loc} in {travel} minutes and arrive at {format_time(arrival)}."
            new_schedule.append(travel_msg)
            # If you arrive early, add a wait message.
            if arrival < friend["start"]:

                new_schedule.append(wait_msg)
            # Add meeting message.

            # Prepare new state: update visited count.
            old_count = start_state["visited_count"]
            start_state["visited_count"] = old_count + 1

            # Prepare new remaining dictionary.
            new_remaining = deepcopy(remaining)
            del new_remaining[friend_name]
            dfs(friend_loc, meeting_finish, new_remaining, new_schedule)

            # Backtrack visited count.
            start_state["visited_count"] = old_count

SOLUTION:
One way to “solve” this problem is to think of it as a “time‐window scheduling” (or “orienteering”) problem. In our case we have a starting location (Pacific Heights at 9:00AM) and five friends—each at a different neighborhood with a fixed availability window and a “minimum meeting duration.” In addition we have travel times (which are not necessarily symmetric) between any two of the locations. Our goal is to plan a route (i.e. an ordering of visits) so that you “meet as many friends as possible” while obeying all constraints:
 
• When traveling from one location to the next, you add the travel time to your current time.
 
• When you arrive at a friend’s location you may have to wait until that friend’s availability starts. Then you “meet” for the required duration. (In our “step‐by‐step” narration we include a message if you have to wait.)
 
• For a meeting to be valid the meeting start time (which is the later of your arrival time and the friend’s available‐from time) plus the friend’s required meeting duration must be less than or equal to that friend’s “available‐until” time.
 
• Finally, because some friends’ windows simply do not let you meet the full minimum duration (for example, Patricia at Embarcadero is available from 7:15AM to 10:15AM meaning that—even if you reach immediately—you cannot squeeze 120 minutes of meeting time after a 9:00AM start), the “feasible” ordering may involve only a subset (in our case Jason, John, Jeffrey and Stephanie).

A generalizable solution method is therefore to:
1. Represent each friend by a dictionary of location, start time, end time (all converted into “minutes‐since‐midnight”) and required meeting duration.
2. Represent the travel times between districts as a “directed graph” (a dictionary of dictionaries).
3. Write a function that, given a starting location and time plus an ordered list of friend visits, “simulates” the day:
  – For each friend, add the travel time from your current location to that friend’s meeting location.
  – If you arrive before the friend’s available‐from time then you “wait” until that time.
  – Then “meet” the friend (making sure that the meeting can finish before the friend’s available‐until time).
  – Update your current time and location.
4. Search among all possible orders (including the possibility of skipping some friends) the order which “meets the most friends”. (In our case, testing all subsets and all orders, we find that the best schedule meets 4 friends.)
5. Finally, take the best schedule and “output” a list of messages describing the itinerary. (For example, the step “You start at …”, “You travel in … minutes …”, “You wait until …”, “You meet … for … minutes from … to …”.)

For instance, one schedule that works is:
 Start at Pacific Heights (9:00AM),
 then travel to Presidio (11 minutes) and wait until 12:45PM to meet Jason for 90 minutes (12:45–2:15PM),
 then travel (26 minutes) to Mission District and wait until John’s window at 6:30PM to meet him for 15 minutes (6:30–6:45PM),
 then travel (19 minutes) to Marina District to meet Jeffrey from about 7:04PM to 8:04PM (his window is 7:00–9:15PM),
 and finally travel (12 minutes) to Nob Hill, wait until 9:45PM and meet Stephanie for 30 minutes (9:45–10:15PM).

Below is a complete Python script that implements the approach described. (You could later generalize it further to solve similar “time‐window” or “orienteering” problems.) 

––––– Begin Script –––––

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import itertools
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

# ---------- Helper Functions ----------

def minutes_to_time(mins):
    # Converts minutes since midnight (0–1439) to a formatted time like "9:00AM" or "2:15PM".
    hour = mins // 60
    minute = mins % 60
    suffix = "AM" if hour < 12 else "PM"
    hour_mod = hour if 1 <= hour <= 12 else hour - 12 if hour > 12 else 12
    return f"{hour_mod}:{minute:02d}{suffix}"

# ---------- Data Definitions ----------

# Travel times (in minutes) from one district to another.
# (Note: these are directed travel times.)
travel_times = {
    "Pacific Heights": {"Embarcadero": 10, "Nob Hill": 8, "Mission District": 15, "Presidio": 11, "Marina District": 6},
    "Embarcadero": {"Pacific Heights": 11, "Nob Hill": 10, "Mission District": 20, "Presidio": 20, "Marina District": 12},
    "Nob Hill": {"Pacific Heights": 8, "Embarcadero": 9, "Mission District": 13, "Presidio": 17, "Marina District": 11},
    "Mission District": {"Pacific Heights": 16, "Embarcadero": 19, "Nob Hill": 12, "Presidio": 25, "Marina District": 19},
    "Presidio": {"Pacific Heights": 11, "Embarcadero": 20, "Nob Hill": 18, "Mission District": 26, "Marina District": 10},
    "Marina District": {"Pacific Heights": 7, "Embarcadero": 14, "Nob Hill": 12, "Mission District": 20, "Presidio": 10}
}

# Friends definition: each friend has a meeting location, available window (start, end) and required duration.
# Times are converted to minutes since midnight.
# 9:00AM = 540 minutes, for example.
friends = {
    "Patricia": {"location": "Embarcadero", "start": 7*60+15, "end": 10*60+15, "duration": 120},
    "Stephanie": {"location": "Nob Hill", "start": 21*60+45, "end": 22*60+15, "duration": 30},
    "John": {"location": "Mission District", "start": 18*60+30, "end": 20*60+30, "duration": 15},
    "Jason": {"location": "Presidio", "start": 12*60+45, "end": 19*60+45, "duration": 90},
    "Jeffrey": {"location": "Marina District", "start": 19*60, "end": 21*60+15, "duration": 60},
}

# Start information:
start_location = "Pacific Heights"
start_time = 9 * 60  # 9:00AM

# ---------- Scheduling Simulation Function ----------

def simulate_schedule(order):
    """
    Given an ordering (list of friend names), simulate the day.
    Returns a tuple (steps, finish_time, count) if the ordering is feasible;
    otherwise returns None.
    """
    steps = []
    # record starting step
    steps.append(f'You start at {start_location} at {minutes_to_time(start_time)}.')
    current_time = start_time
    current_loc = start_location
    
    for friend in order:
        friend_info = friends[friend]
        target = friend_info["location"]
        # get travel time (if path not found, discard order)
        if current_loc not in travel_times or target not in travel_times[current_loc]:
            return None
        travel = travel_times[current_loc][target]
        arrival_time = current_time + travel
        steps.append(f'You travel to {target} in {travel} minutes and arrive at {minutes_to_time(arrival_time)}.')
        
        # If we arrive before the friend is available, wait
        if arrival_time < friend_info["start"]:
            steps.append(f'You wait until {minutes_to_time(friend_info["start"])}.')
            meeting_start = friend_info["start"]
        else:
            meeting_start = arrival_time

        meeting_end = meeting_start + friend_info["duration"]
        # Check if the meeting can be completed before the friend’s “available‐until” time.
        if meeting_end > friend_info["end"]:
            return None   # meeting not possible; discard this ordering

        steps.append(f'You meet {friend} for {friend_info["duration"]} minutes from {minutes_to_time(meeting_start)} to {minutes_to_time(meeting_end)}.')
        # Update current time and location
        current_time = meeting_end
        current_loc = target

    return steps, current_time, len(order)

# ---------- Search for the Best Schedule ----------

best_schedule = None
max_friends_met = 0
earliest_finish = None

# We try all non-empty subsets (all possible orders in which you could meet a subset of friends).
all_friend_names = list(friends.keys())
# Try orders of lengths 1 to len(friends)
for r in range(1, len(all_friend_names)+1):
    for order in itertools.permutations(all_friend_names, r):
        sim = simulate_schedule(order)
        if sim is not None:
            steps, finish_time, count = sim
            # Choose the order that meets the most friends.
            # If there is a tie we take the one that finishes earliest.
            if count > max_friends_met or (count == max_friends_met and (earliest_finish is None or finish_time < earliest_finish)):
                best_schedule = steps
                max_friends_met = count
                earliest_finish = finish_time

# ---------- Print the Best Schedule ----------

if best_schedule:
    # Here is our itinerary as a list of strings.
    print(best_schedule)
else:
    print("No feasible schedule was found.")

One way to “solve” this problem is to think of it as a “time‐window scheduling” (or “orienteering”) problem. In our case we have a starting location (Pacific Heights at 9:00AM) and five friends—each at a different neighborhood with a fixed availability window and a “minimum meeting duration.” In addition we have travel times (which are not necessarily symmetric) between any two of the locations. Our goal is to plan a route (i.e. an ordering of visits) so that you “meet as many friends as possible” while obeying all constraints:
 
• When traveling from one location to the next, you add the travel time to your current time.
 
• When you arrive at a friend’s location you may have to wait until that friend’s availability starts. Then you “meet” for the required duration. (In our “step‐by‐step” narration we include a message if you have to wait.)
 
• For a meeting to be valid the meeting start time (which is the later of your arrival time and the friend’s available‐from time) plus the friend’s required meeting duration must be less than or equal to that friend’s “available‐until” time.
 
• Finally, because some friends’ windows simply do not let you meet the full minimum duration (for example, Patricia at Embarcadero is available from 7:15AM to 10:15AM meaning that—even if you reach immediately—you cannot squeeze 120 minutes of meeting time after a 9:00AM start), the “feasible” ordering may involve only a subset (in our case Jason, John, Jeffrey and Stephanie).

1. Represent each friend by a dictionary of location, start time, end time (all converted into “minutes‐since‐midnight”) and required meeting duration.
2. Represent the travel times between districts as a “directed graph” (a dictionary of dictionaries).

  – For each friend, add the travel time from your current location to that friend’s meeting location.
  – If you arrive before the friend’s available‐from time then you “wait” until that time.
  – Then “meet” the friend (making sure that the meeting can finish before the friend’s available‐until time).

We can solve this problem by “modeling” it as a time‐window scheduling problem with travel times between “nodes” (the different San Francisco locations). In our case the “nodes” are the locations where your friends will be. Each friend “i” is available between a start and end time and requires a minimum meeting duration. You begin at Golden Gate Park at 9:00AM. In moving between locations you have to add a travel time (which depends on the starting and destination locations) and, if you arrive before the friend’s available start time, you must wait until that time.

One general method is to try different orderings (schedules) of the friend visits. For each ordering you “simulate” your day:
1. Start at Golden Gate Park at 9:00AM.
2. For each friend in the chosen order, add the travel time from your current location to that friend’s location.
3. If you arrive before your friend is available, you wait until the friend’s available start time.
4. You then “meet” the friend for the required minimum time. (If meeting cannot be completed before the friend’s available window ends, then this order is not valid.)
5. Update your current time and location, and proceed to the next friend.

Since your objective is to “meet as many friends as possible” (and all five friends are in play) you can choose the ordering that is feasible and (optionally) minimizes “waiting time.”

For example, one schedule that works is:
– Start at Golden Gate Park at 9:00AM.
– Travel 16 minutes to Pacific Heights and arrive at 9:16AM. (Stephanie is available from 7:15AM so you immediately meet her for her 15‐minute minimum from 9:16AM to 9:31AM.)
– From Pacific Heights travel 12 minutes to Union Square arriving at 9:43AM. (Jeffrey is available since 7:45AM so you meet him for 60 minutes from 9:43AM to 10:43AM.)
– Then travel 11 minutes from Union Square to Embarcadero arriving at 10:54AM. (But Paul is only available starting at 12:30PM so you wait until then and meet him for 30 minutes from 12:30PM to 1:00PM.)
– Next travel 21 minutes from Embarcadero to Haight-Ashbury arriving at 1:21PM. (Mary is available only from 4:45PM so you wait until 4:45PM and meet her for 30 minutes until 5:15PM.)
– Finally travel 15 minutes from Haight-Ashbury to Presidio arriving at 5:30PM. (John becomes available at 6:30PM so you wait until then and meet him for 45 minutes from 6:30PM to 7:15PM.)

This schedule meets all the friends’ time windows and the required meeting durations. (There is considerable “waiting time” – but since the main goal is to meet everyone and not to minimize idle time, this schedule optimizes your goal.)

Below is a complete Python script that (i) defines the travel times and friend availabilities, (ii) “simulates” the day for every ordering of the friend visits and chooses the one that meets all meetings (i.e. all five) with the lowest total waiting time, and (iii) outputs the full schedule in a list of strings as shown in the example.

# Helper function: Convert minutes-since-midnight to 12-hour clock string.

    hour = minutes // 60

    elif hour == 12:
        display_hour = 12
        suffix = "PM"

        suffix = "PM"
    else:

    }
}

    current_time = start_time
    current_location = start_location
    total_wait = 0
    events = []
    
    events.append(f"You start at {start_location} at {format_time(current_time)}.")
    
    for friend in order:
        friend_loc = friend_data[friend]["location"]
        # Get travel time from current location to friend location.
        travel = travel_times[current_location][friend_loc]
        arrival_time = current_time + travel
        events.append(f"You travel to {friend_loc} in {travel} minutes and arrive at {format_time(arrival_time)}.")
        
        # Determine if we need to wait for the friend to be available.
        friend_avail_start = friend_data[friend]["avail_start"]
        if arrival_time < friend_avail_start:
            wait = friend_avail_start - arrival_time
            total_wait += wait
            events.append(f"You wait until {format_time(friend_avail_start)}.")
            meeting_start = friend_avail_start
        else:
            meeting_start = arrival_time
        
        # Schedule the meeting.
        meet_time = friend_data[friend]["min_meet"]
        meeting_end = meeting_start + meet_time
        
        # Check if meeting can be completed in friend’s window.
        if meeting_end > friend_data[friend]["avail_end"]:
            # Not a valid schedule.
            return None, None, None
        
        events.append(f"You meet {friend} for {meet_time} minutes from {format_time(meeting_start)} to {format_time(meeting_end)}.")
        
        # Update current time and location.
        current_time = meeting_end
        current_location = friend_loc

    return total_wait, current_time, events

# List all friend names.

# Try all orderings and choose one that meets all friends (max count) and minimizes waiting.

        # All 5 meetings are scheduled.
        if total_wait < min_total_wait:

            best_schedule = events
            best_order = order

# If a best schedule is found, print it.

    print(schedule_output)
else:
    print("No valid schedule found.")

One way to solve “friend‐meet scheduling” problems – which combine time‐window feasibility, mandatory meeting durations, and travel times – is to treat the problem as a kind of “time‐window routing” or “TSP with time windows” problem. In our example each friend is represented by a meeting “task” with:
 • a location,
 • an available time window (start and end times), and
 • a required meeting duration.
You start at a given location (here Bayview at 9:00AM) and you have a travel‐time “matrix” that tells you how long it takes to get from one spot to another.

A general solution method is as follows:
1. Represent each friend as a “task” with fields: name, location, available‐start time, available‐end time, and required meeting duration. Also represent the travel times in a dictionary (or matrix) where, for example, travel[“Bayview”][“Union Square”] = 17.
2. Given that the objective is to “meet as many friends as possible,” the idea is to test different orders (or subsets) of friend meetings. In our small problem (six friends) we can simply generate every permutation of the friend list and “simulate” the day.
3. For a given permutation, start at Bayview at 9:00AM. Then for each friend in the order:
  a. Compute the travel time from the current location to that friend’s location.
  b. Determine the arrival time and, if you arrive early (before your friend’s available start), wait until that time.
  c. Start the meeting at the later of the travel‐arrival time and the friend’s available start, and check that the meeting can last for the required duration before the friend’s available end.
  d. If the meeting fits in the time window, “record” a step in your schedule (including travel, waiting, and meeting strings) and update your current location and time.
4. If at any step you cannot fit the full meeting, then the schedule for that permutation “ends” and you record the number of friends successfully met.
5. Finally, pick the schedule (i.e. friend ordering) that gives the maximum number of meetings. (If several schedules yield the same maximum, you may choose, for example, the one that finishes earliest.)

SOLUTION:
We can view the problem as a “time‐window scheduling with travel times” or a “time–dependent traveling salesman” problem. In our case the “nodes” are your friends’ neighborhoods. Each friend has a time window (for example Joseph is “open” at Bayview from 12:15PM until 8:15PM) and a minimum meeting‐duration. Starting from Pacific Heights at 9:00AM, you must decide in which order to visit the friends. Between each “visit” you incur a travel time that depends on both your current location and the next friend’s location. In addition, if you arrive early (before the friend’s start time) you must wait. Finally, for a meeting to be valid the meeting must “fit” inside the friend’s available window.

A generalizable solution method is as follows:
1. Represent the travel times between every pair of nodes (locations) in a lookup table.
2. Represent each friend by a data record containing:
  • Name (e.g. “Joseph”)
  • Location (e.g. “Bayview”)
  • Availability start and end times (converted into minutes since midnight for easy calculations)
  • Required meeting duration.
3. Start at your fixed starting point (Pacific Heights at 9:00AM) and simulate a route—that is, given an order in which to visit the friends, do:
  a. Compute the travel time from your current location to the next friend’s location.
  b. Update your “arrival time.” If you reach before the friend’s availability starts, you must wait.
  c. Schedule the meeting (ensuring that the meeting’s end time, which is the effective start plus the meeting duration, does not exceed the friend’s availability).
  d. Update your current time and location.  
4. Since there are only 6 friends, you can enumerate all possible orders (720 of them) to check which orders allow you to “meet” the greatest number of friends. (In our case one order meeting all 6 friends is possible.)
5. Finally, choose the optimal order (here we also break ties by, say, finishing earlier) and output the schedule in the desired instruction‐format.  
For example, one valid optimal schedule is:
  • Start at Pacific Heights at 9:00AM.
  • Travel to The Castro (David’s location) – 16 minutes (arrive 9:16AM), meet David for 45 minutes (9:16AM–10:01AM).
  • Travel to Presidio (Rebecca) – 20 minutes (arrive 10:21AM) but wait until 11:00AM; then meet Rebecca for 105 minutes (11:00AM–12:45PM).
  • Travel to Bayview (Joseph) – 31 minutes (arrive 1:16PM), meet Joseph for 45 minutes (1:16PM–2:01PM).
  • Travel to Alamo Square (Laura) – 16 minutes (arrive 2:17PM), meet Laura for 75 minutes (2:17PM–3:32PM).
  • Travel to Russian Hill (Andrew) – 13 minutes (arrive 3:45PM), meet Andrew for 60 minutes (3:45PM–4:45PM).
  • Travel to Financial District (Carol) – 11 minutes (arrive 4:56PM) and wait until 5:30PM; meet Carol for 30 minutes (5:30PM–6:00PM).

Below is a complete Python script that implements the above method. (Note that because the problem size is small, we “brute–force” through all permutations to find the best schedule.)

 • an available time window (start and end times, expressed in minutes from 9:00AM), and

def minutes_to_time(t):
    """
    Convert minutes since midnight into a time string with the format H:MMAM/PM.
    """
    hour = t // 60
    minute = t % 60
    period = "AM"
    if hour >= 12:
        period = "PM"
        if hour > 12:
            hour -= 12
    if hour == 0:
        hour = 12
    return f"{hour}:{minute:02d}{period}"

SOLUTION:
One way to solve a “friend‐meeting scheduling” problem is to “treat” it as a variant of the Traveling Salesman Problem with Time Windows and service (meeting) durations. In our case we start at Mission District at 9:00AM and we have a set of friends –each at a different San Francisco neighborhood– with given available time windows and minimum meeting durations. In addition, we know the travel time (in minutes) between every pair of locations (and note that travel times may be asymmetric).

A general method is as follows:
1. Define your “nodes” (friends’ meeting appointments) with the following attributes:
  • location (e.g. Chinatown, Pacific Heights, …)
  • availability window [start, end] (expressed as minutes after 9:00AM; for example, 12:00PM becomes 180 minutes)
  • required service (meeting) duration.
  For friends whose available start is before 9:00AM (like Joseph, available from 8:00AM), you use the maximum of that start and your arrival time.
2. Store the travel times between every pair of locations (including your starting “node” at Mission District).
3. Then use a “depth‐first search (DFS)” or backtracking algorithm that, from your current location and time, tries every possible next friend that you have not yet visited. For each potential friend you:
  a. Compute the travel time (by looking up the travel time dictionary) and determine your arrival time at that friend’s location.
  b. Determine the meeting “start time” as the later of the arrival and the friend’s available start.
  c. Check that if you add the required meeting duration, the meeting will finish by the friend’s available end.
  d. If so, save the travel event (with the “travel to” and “arrival” time), note any waiting time if you arrived earlier than the friend’s start time, and then record the meeting event.
  e. Then call DFS recursively from this friend’s location at the new “current time” (the finishing time of the meeting).
4. Over all possible orders the algorithm “picks” the schedule (or friend–visit sequence) that meets the most friends. (In our instance the available friends come in two “conflicting pairs” –one early pair (Patricia versus Ronald) and one in the afternoon (John versus Jeffrey) – so the best you can do is to schedule six meetings.)
5. Finally, after the DFS finishes you output your (best) schedule as a list of strings describing each event. For example, an event might say: 
  "You travel to Financial District in 15 minutes and arrive at 9:15AM." etc.

To solve a problem like this we can model it as a “time‐window scheduling” or “vehicle routing with time windows” problem. In general, you can follow these steps:

1. Define each meeting (node) with its location, available time window, and the minimum meeting duration required.
2. Represent travel times between locations as directed edges.
3. Start at your initial location and time (Pacific Heights at 9:00AM). Then, for each friend you plan to meet, compute the arrival time as:
  arrival_time = previous_finish_time + travel_time.
4. If you arrive before the friend’s availability begins, add a waiting period until the start time.
5. Then “service” the meeting by using the minimum time required; that is, the meeting must extend for at least the specified duration.
6. Continue to the next friend so that the meeting’s end time plus the travel time fits within that friend’s available time window.
7. Use search or backtracking to consider different permutations of the meetings in order to maximize the total number of friends met.

The idea is to “simulate” a schedule by starting at Chinatown at time 0. Then, for a chosen order (an “itinerary”) of friends we compute:
 1. From the current location and current time, add the travel time to the next friend’s venue.
 2. If you arrive before that friend’s availability (earlier than the “start” of their window), you wait.
 3. You then “meet” that friend for the required duration provided the meeting ends by the friend’s “end time.”
 4. Update the “current time” to the end of the meeting and the “current location” to that friend’s venue.
 5. Continue with the next friend in the itinerary.

Because not every friend’s time window is compatible with every other (for example, some windows are very short – Mark and Emily, or George’s window is “tight”) we may not be able to meet everyone. Thus our goal is to pick the maximum‐cardinality set of friends (the “best schedule”) that can be visited in some order subject to the travel+waiting+meeting time constraints.

One generalizable solution method is:
 a. Represent each friend by a record (name, location, window_start, window_end, duration) and represent travel times as a dictionary keyed by (from_location, to_location).
 b. For each candidate ordering (or, equivalently, for each subset of friends and order of visiting them) simulate the day:
  – Start at “Chinatown” (time 0, which corresponds to 9:00AM).

We can “model” the problem as a time‐window scheduling problem with travel “lag” between appointments. In our case we have a start location (Chinatown at 9:00AM, which we treat as time zero) and a list of friends. Each friend is associated with:
 • a meeting location,
 • an “availability window” (start and end times – note that we convert clock‐times into “minutes after 9:00AM”; for example, 1:45PM becomes 285 minutes and 5:30PM becomes 510 minutes),
 • a minimum meeting duration.

Also, a table of travel times is given (note that the travel time “from A to B” may differ from “B to A”).

The idea is to “simulate” a schedule by starting at Chinatown at time 0. Then, for a chosen order (an “itinerary”) of friends we compute:
 1. From the current location and current time, add the travel time to the next friend’s venue.
 2. If you arrive before that friend’s availability (earlier than the “start” of their window), you wait.
 3. You then “meet” that friend for the required duration provided the meeting ends by the friend’s “end time.”
 4. Update the “current time” to the end of the meeting and the “current location” to that friend’s venue.
 5. Continue with the next friend in the itinerary.

Because not every friend’s time window is compatible with every other (for example, some windows are very short – Mark and Emily, or George’s window is “tight”) we may not be able to meet everyone. Thus our goal is to pick the maximum‐cardinality set of friends (the “best schedule”) that can be visited in some order subject to the travel+waiting+meeting time constraints.

One generalizable solution method is:
 a. Represent each friend by a record (name, location, window_start, window_end, duration) and represent travel times as a dictionary keyed by (from_location, to_location).
 b. For each candidate ordering (or, equivalently, for each subset of friends and order of visiting them) simulate the day:
  – Start at “Chinatown” (time 0, which corresponds to 9:00AM).
  – For each friend in order, compute arrival = current_time + travel_time(from_current, friend.location). Then let meeting_start = max(arrival, friend.window_start). If meeting_start + meeting_duration ≤ friend.window_end, the meeting is feasible; otherwise the ordering fails.
  – Record the “step‐strings” (for example, “You travel to X …” or “You wait until …” or “You meet Y …”).
  – Continue until all meetings in that ordering are simulated.
 c. Among all candidate orders, pick the schedule that “meets” the greatest number of friends.

 1. Start at Chinatown at 9:00AM.
 2. Travel to Golden Gate Park (travel time 23 minutes), wait until 1:45PM (Melissa’s window opens), meet Melissa for 90 minutes (from 1:45PM to 3:15PM).
 3. Travel to Pacific Heights (16 minutes) and meet Mark for 45 minutes (from about 3:31PM to 4:16PM – Mark is available 3:00PM–5:00PM).

 6. Finally, travel to Fisherman’s Wharf (7 minutes) and meet Margaret for 15 minutes (from 7:41PM to 7:56PM – Margaret is available 2:45PM–8:15PM).

Such a schedule visits five friends. (Other orders – for example those involving George or Rebecca rather than Melissa – were considered; however, due to overlapping and “tight” time windows, the maximum count turns out to be five.)

We can “model” the day as a scheduling‐orienteering problem with time–windows. In our general approach we do the following:

1. Define each “meeting” (friend) by its location, the time‐window during which the meeting can happen, and the minimum duration needed. (For example, Kimberly is at Union Square from 6:00PM to 7:30PM and you need 75 minutes with her.) Also list the travel times between every pair of locations (note that travel times are not symmetric).

2. Represent the overall state by the current location and the current time (we begin at Embarcadero at 9:00AM, which we convert to minutes “540”). When “traveling” from one location to the next, add the travel time. Then if you arrive before a friend’s window starts, you must “wait” until the friend is available. The meeting then is scheduled starting at max(arrival_time, friend_available_start) and lasts that friend’s minimum meeting time; and it must finish before the friend’s window closes.

3. Using a backtracking (or recursive depth‐first search) method, try every ordering (permutation) of friends. At each step, check:
  • if you travel from your current location and time to a friend’s location, what time would you arrive?
  • if you must wait until the friend’s available start time, then start the meeting at that max(arrival, window_start).
  • if the meeting (i.e. start time plus minimum meeting duration) finishes before the friend’s available window ends, then this friend can be “visited.”
  • update the current time to the meeting end and your location to that friend’s spot.

4. Among all “reachable” orders (each order is a sequence of “actions” – travel, wait if needed, and meetings), choose the one that meets the maximum number of friends (our objective is to “meet as many friends as possible”). For example, one candidate schedule is to visit:

SOLUTION:
One way to approach this kind of “day‐planner” problem is to treat it as a scheduling (or “travelling salesman with time windows”) problem. In a general solution you would:

1. List each “friend–location” with its available time window and the minimum meeting duration. For example, Betty is at Russian Hill from 7:00AM until 4:45PM and requires 105 minutes, Melissa is at Alamo Square with a window 9:30AM–5:15PM (105 minutes needed), Joshua is at Haight‐Ashbury from 12:15PM–7:00PM (90 minutes minimum), and so on.

2. Represent the travel times between locations (note they are directional) using a dictionary or matrix.

3. Knowing that you begin at a fixed “start node” (Union Square at 9:00AM), you generate candidate orders (or use a backtracking/optimization algorithm) that sequence visits to friends so that:
  – You can travel from one location to the next (with the given travel times),
  – You may have to wait until a friend is “available” if you arrive early,
  – The meeting (which lasts the required minimum minutes) is completely contained inside that friend’s available window.

4. Then among all feasible orders you choose one that “meets as many friends as possible” (this is our “objective function”). In our example it turns out that, because several friends’ windows overlap very tightly (for instance, Anthony at Chinatown is only available 11:45AM–1:30PM and Timothy’s window is similarly narrow) you cannot visit all eight friends. In fact, by exploring various sequences you determine that – under the travel‐and‐meeting constraints – the maximum number you can schedule is six.

A sample “optimal” schedule that meets six friends is one that visits these locations (and friends):
  • Melissa at Alamo Square,
  • Anthony at Chinatown,
  • Betty at Russian Hill,
  • Jeffrey at Marina District,
  • Joshua at Haight‐Ashbury,
  • Emily at Sunset District.

For example, the schedule can work out as follows (times are computed by adding travel durations and meeting durations to your start time):

• You leave Union Square at 9:00AM and travel 15 minutes to Alamo Square;
  – arrive around 9:15AM, wait until 9:30AM (Melissa’s available start), then meet Melissa for 105 minutes (9:30AM–11:15AM).

• Next, you travel 15 minutes from Alamo Square to Chinatown;
  – arriving 11:15AM+15 = 11:30AM, wait until Anthony is available at 11:45AM and meet him for 75 minutes (11:45AM–1:00PM).

• Then you travel 7 minutes from Chinatown to Russian Hill;
  – arriving at about 1:00PM+7 = 1:07PM and meet Betty (105 minutes) from 1:07PM to about 2:52PM.

• You then travel 7 minutes from Russian Hill to the Marina District;
  – arriving around 2:52PM+7 = 2:59PM and meet Jeffrey for 45 minutes (roughly 2:59PM–3:44PM).

• Next, you take a 16‐minute ride from the Marina District to Haight‐Ashbury;
  – arriving about 3:44PM+16 = 4:00PM and meet Joshua for 90 minutes (4:00PM–5:30PM).

• Finally, you travel 15 minutes from Haight–Ashbury to the Sunset District;
  – arriving around 5:30PM+15 = 5:45PM; you then wait until Emily’s window opens at 7:30PM and meet her for 120 minutes (7:30PM–9:30PM).

This schedule satisfies every friend’s availability. (Notice that because Emily’s available window is very “late‐in‐the‐day”, if you add an extra friend before her then even with the best travel times you would end up arriving too late to complete her full 120–minute meeting.)

  c. Then “meet” the friend for the required duration. (Make sure that the meeting finishes by the friend’s available end time.)
  d. Update your current time and location to the end of that meeting.

In our formulation each friend is “served” at a specific location (for example, Sandra is at the Richmond District) and is only available during a given time window (for example, Sandra is available from 7:00AM to 9:15PM) and you must “service” that node for at least the minimum meeting duration. Travel between locations is “directed” (the travel time from Alamo Square to another location may differ from the return) and, when you arrive before a friend’s window opens, you must wait.

One general‐approach is to model the day as a “time–windowed route‐planning” problem. In our case each friend is a “node” that has:
  •  a location,
  •  a time–window (available start and end time, expressed nicely as minutes since midnight), and 
  •  a minimum meeting (service) duration.
Also, we have travel times between every pair of neighborhoods. Starting at Nob Hill at 9:00AM (which we represent as 540 minutes after midnight), we “visit” friends in some order. When going from your current location at the current time to a friend’s location, you add the travel time from your table. When you arrive you might have to wait (if you are “too early”) until the friend’s available start time. Then you “meet” the friend for their required duration. (This meeting must finish before the friend’s end time.) 

We can use a depth‐first search (DFS) algorithm. At each “state” we keep track of:
  – the current location,
  – the current time,
  – and which friends have already been met.
Then for each friend not yet met we check:
 1. How long it takes to get there from the current location.
 2. Use arrival = current_time + travel_time.
 3. Define meeting_start = max(arrival, friend’s window start). (This incorporates waiting if you arrive too early.)
 4. Then meeting_end = meeting_start + meeting duration.
 5. If meeting_end is within the friend’s available window, then that “visit” is feasible.
We append the descriptive “event” lines (for travel, waiting, and meeting) to the schedule and then call DFS recursively from the new state.
Finally, we choose the schedule that “visits” the maximum number of friends.

One general‐approach is to model the day as a “time–windowed route‐planning” problem. In our case each friend is a “node” that has:
  •  a location,

Also, we have travel times between every pair of neighborhoods. Starting at Nob Hill at 9:00AM (which we represent as 540 minutes after midnight), we “visit” friends in some order. When going from your current location at the current time to a friend’s location, you add the travel time from your table. When you arrive you might have to wait (if you are “too early”) until the friend’s available start time. Then you “meet” the friend for their required duration. (This meeting must finish before the friend’s end time.) 

We can use a depth‐first search (DFS) algorithm. At each “state” we keep track of:
  – the current location,
  – the current time,
  – and which friends have already been met.
Then for each friend not yet met we check:
 1. How long it takes to get there from the current location.
 2. Use arrival = current_time + travel_time.
 3. Define meeting_start = max(arrival, friend’s window start). (This incorporates waiting if you arrive too early.)
 4. Then meeting_end = meeting_start + meeting duration.
 5. If meeting_end is within the friend’s available window, then that “visit” is feasible.
We append the descriptive “event” lines (for travel, waiting, and meeting) to the schedule and then call DFS recursively from the new state.
Finally, we choose the schedule that “visits” the maximum number of friends.
The approach is generalizable to problems where you have a set of time–window constraints and travel times between nodes (a variant of the “vehicle routing problem with time windows”).

After testing several orders we found one feasible schedule that meets 8 friends. (Because the evening time windows for Sandra and Joseph overlap, we must choose one “evening‐slot” pair – here we choose to meet Joseph after a series of mid‐afternoon meetings.) For instance, one possible route is:

One way to attack the problem is to “model” it as a time‐window scheduling/routing problem on a directed graph. In our situation each “node” is a location (for example “Russian Hill” for Jessica) with a constraint: the friend is available only between a start and an end time and you must “meet” for at least a given duration. You begin at “Union Square” at 9:00AM (which we convert to minutes from midnight, i.e. 540 minutes). For each friend you want to visit you must:
 1. Compute the travel time from your current location to that friend’s location. (Note the travel times are not symmetric; for example Union Square→Mission District is 14 minutes while the reverse is 15 minutes.)
 2. Compute your arrival time as current_time + travel_time.
 3. “Wait” if necessary until the friend’s available time window begins. (That is, the meeting can’t start before the friend is available.)
 4. Start the meeting at max(arrival_time, friend.avail_start) and then spend exactly the minimum meeting time.
 5. Check that the meeting finishes before or exactly at the friend’s available end.

Because you wish to maximize the number of friends met, you must try various orders. In a generalizable solution you might run a depth‐first search (DFS) where each state is your current location, the current time and the set of friends you have already met. For each friend not yet visited, if the travel + waiting + meeting time fits inside that friend’s window then you extend your “itinerary” with the travel (possibly with a “wait” step) and the meeting. You then update the current location and time (which is the meeting finish time) and recursively try the remaining friends. Finally, you pick the itinerary (i.e. schedule) that “visits” the largest number of friends.

 3. “Wait” if necessary until the friend’s available time window begins. (That is, the meeting can’t start before the friend is available.)

 5. Check that the meeting finishes before or exactly at the friend’s available end.

We can solve the problem by “tour‐planning” through San Francisco as a time–window scheduling problem with travel times. In our version each friend is associated with:
 • a meeting location (one of “North Beach”, “Chinatown”, “Russian Hill”, etc.),
 • an available time window [start, end] (converted to minutes past midnight),
 • and a meeting “service” time (the minimum minutes you must spend with that friend).

We begin at North Beach at 9:00AM (i.e. 540 minutes after midnight). Whenever we travel to a friend’s location from our current location we add the travel time (based on the table). When arriving at a friend’s location, the earliest meeting start is the later of (a) the arrival time and (b) the friend’s window–start time (if you arrive early you will have to wait). Then, if the meeting duration added to that meeting start time does not exceed the friend’s available window–end, you can “service” that friend successfully. In that case your “departure” time becomes the meeting’s finish time and your location becomes that friend’s district.

Thus the problem becomes: “starting at North Beach at 540 minutes, what ordering of visits (subject to travel and waiting) allows you to meet the maximum number of friends?” This is essentially a vehicle routing problem with time windows (with the objective of maximizing the number of visits rather than minimizing time). Because there are only 10 friends we can simply try all orders using a DFS/backtracking search.

The DFS works as follows:
 1. From the current state (with current location and time), try every friend not already visited.
 2. For each candidate friend, compute the travel time from your current location to that friend’s district.
 3. Calculate the arrival time. If you arrive before the friend’s available window begins, then you must wait until the friend’s start time.
 4. Your confirmed meeting start time is the maximum of arrival and the friend’s start. Add the friend’s meeting duration; if the finish time is within the friend’s window, then you can “meet” that friend. (Record the “travel”, “wait” [if needed], and “meeting” messages.)
 5. Recursively continue from the new state (new location, new current time, with that friend marked as visited).

def dfs(current_time, current_loc, visited, schedule):
    best_count = len(visited)
    best_schedule = schedule[:]
    
    # Try to visit any friend not yet visited.
    for i, friend in enumerate(friends):
        if i in visited:
            continue
        travel = travel_times[current_loc][friend["location"]]
        arrival = current_time + travel
        # If you arrive before the friend’s available window, you wait.
        meeting_start = max(arrival, friend["start"])
        meeting_end = meeting_start + friend["duration"]
        
        # Check if meeting fits inside friend’s available window.
        if meeting_end <= friend["end"]:
            new_schedule = schedule[:]
            # Add a travel step message.
            travel_msg = f"You travel to {friend['location']} in {travel} minutes and arrive at {minutes_to_time(arrival)}."
            new_schedule.append(travel_msg)
            # If you had to wait for the friend’s start time, document that.
            if arrival < friend["start"]:
                wait_msg = f"You wait until {minutes_to_time(meeting_start)}."
                new_schedule.append(wait_msg)
            meet_msg = f"You meet {friend['name']} for {friend['duration']} minutes from {minutes_to_time(meeting_start)} to {minutes_to_time(meeting_end)}."
            new_schedule.append(meet_msg)
            
            # Recursively try to plan the next meeting.
            new_visited = visited.union({i})
            count, cand_schedule = dfs(meeting_end, friend["location"], new_visited, new_schedule)
            if count > best_count:
                best_count = count
                best_schedule = cand_schedule[:]
    return best_count, best_schedule
